俄國物理學家李昂·特雷門於1920年10月發明特雷門，源自蘇聯政府支持近接感測研: The Russian physicist Léon Theremin invented the theremin in October 1920, out of Soviet government-supported research into proximity sensing, and took a US patent in 1928. After touring Europe he went to the United States and licensed production to the Radio Corporation of America; the theremin came out in 1929, did not sell well but drew listeners. That year Joseph Schillinger wrote a Suite for Theremin and Orchestra for it, played by the inventor. After the Second World War it declined as easier-to-play electronic instruments appeared, and was carried on by electronics hobbyists and kit builders; Robert Moog made and sold kits.
特雷門屬電鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 531.1。其發聲不靠實體接: The theremin is an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 531.1. It sounds without physical contact: the player moves a hand towards the vertical metal rod to change the pitch and towards the horizontal loop to change the volume; the further the hand from the volume antenna, the louder the sound. Because pitch is controlled continuously by capacitive position sensing, with no visible keys or fingering marks, the timbre changes continuously without fixed steps, and the player sets the intonation entirely by feel. The source notes that its sound is often associated with eerie situations, and early films used it to create an atmosphere of horror. Compared with instruments that must be touched to be played, the difference is that the position of the body directly controls an oscillating circuit.
特雷門為電鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 531.1，地區為歐洲: The theremin is an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 531.1, from Europe / Russia. It is played without holding or touching the instrument: the player stands in front of two metal antennas, usually the right hand controlling pitch and the left the volume. The distance between hand and antenna changes the capacitance and so the oscillating circuit, and this makes the sound. For a higher note, move the hand closer to the pitch antenna; for more volume, move it away from the volume antenna. Since the position of the hand leaves no visible mark, a beginner must control intonation by feel.

The theremin is an electronic instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs number 531.1. Its player is called a thereminist and stands in front of two metal antennas, one a long straight rod and one a horizontal loop, changing the capacitance without touching them: one side controls pitch, the other volume, and the signal is amplified and comes out of a loudspeaker. The usual arrangement is the right hand for pitch and the left for volume, though some players reverse it. It is used in the concert hall for classical repertoire, and to create an atmosphere of horror in early film; electronics hobbyists and kit builders use it too, and it is seen as a route into music making for people with physical disabilities.
